configs.label: phase3
configs.description: Phase 3 retrieval: BM25 without stemming or expansion, RRF k=60 with equal weights, the settings' cross-encoder, no priors.

configs.label: tuned
configs.description: Frozen 2026-10-13, chosen on the DEV split only (no TEST question was ranked or scored): highest dev nDCG@10 of hybrid_rerank (tie-break recall@10), preferring fewer non-default options within 0.01 (docs/rag-tuning.md). Options: date_prior 3, statement_boost 1.5, year_prior 1.25, recency_prior 1 with a 90-day half-life. Everything else is phase3: BM25 without stemming or query expansion, RRF k=60 with equal weights, 50 candidates, and the MiniLM-L-6 cross-encoder, pinned here to the commit the settings use so the preset does not follow a RERANKER_MODEL change. The production default (RETRIEVER_PRESET) since the one TEST evaluation, where the switch rule decided before that run held (docs/rag-tuning.md).

validation.annotator: three Claude Opus 5.5 sessions, not people: C, isolated (it saw only a copy of the sample), and A and B, two earlier sessions whose independence cannot be verified

annotators.description: Claude (claude-opus-5-5), isolated (copied sample only): a later session whose own directory held only a copy of rag_judge_sample.json; it read that copy and the judge prompt's definitions (judge_prompts.py), labelled every slot and saved its labels (sha256 1e48968a...ed08) before opening the key, A's and B's labels, the benchmark file or the caches; blind to the judge's verdicts; not a person
Claude (claude-opus-5-5), independent of the OpenAI judge, blind to the judge's verdicts; labels from the question, cited passages and answer only, following the judge prompt's definitions
Claude (claude-opus-5-5), independent of the gpt-5.5 judge, blind to its verdicts

validation.note: Agreement is on pass/fail verdicts (claims supported; citations supporting fully or in part; facts covered; answer declines or not), exact agreement on the three-way labels; kappa is Cohen's, on pass/fail. Sampled answers by run: phase3/hybrid_rerank 40. C is the main check: it worked in its own directory from a copy of the sample alone and saved its labels before seeing the key or the other labels. A and B gave the same label on all 383 slots; B finished a minute after A, with A's working files in the same scratch directory, so their independence cannot be verified and A vs B says nothing about reproducibility. C vs A measures it: 376 of 383 labels agree. All three are the same model, so judge vs annotator compares gpt-5.5 with Claude, not with a person.

bootstrap.method: Percentile bootstrap over questions: 10,000 resamples drawn with replacement (numpy default_rng seed 20261013), 95% intervals. Each metric uses the questions where it is defined (n). A paired difference resamples the questions once and scores both runs on each resample. Questions are treated as independent draws from the kinds of questions the set covers.

selection.rule: Default-switch rule, decided before the TEST run (self-recorded; no timestamped copy predates it): make tuned the production default instead of phase3 only if, on TEST, (a) the paired-bootstrap 95% CI of hybrid_rerank nDCG@10, tuned minus phase3, lies entirely above 0, and (b) hybrid_rerank answer_correctness is not worse (paired difference, tuned minus phase3, CI lower bound above -0.05). TEST: (a) +0.222 [+0.158, +0.293], n = 50: holds; (b) +0.140 [+0.068, +0.218], n = 50: holds. Both hold, so tuned is chosen. The tuned preset itself was frozen on DEV only (docs/rag-tuning.md); TEST only decided the switch.

notes: Retrieval metrics are expected values over the orders of tied scores (McSherry and Najork, 2008): fused rankings often tie, and the fusion's tie-break is arbitrary.

Retrieval latency is measured per question after a warm-up query, with the query embedding served from a local cache: the OpenAI embedding round trip that dense, hybrid and hybrid_rerank pay in the API is not included. Answer latency adds the LLM call.
Answer metrics come from an LLM judge, not from people. The judge check compares its verdicts with annotators' labels on a blind sample and says which annotators worked in isolation.

Known judge errors, found by reading tuned answers against their passages; the metrics keep the judge's verdicts. ua-03: a correct decline marked as fabricated (with it corrected, tuned refusal accuracy is 5/5 and faithfulness 0.956). pp-03: an answer about the wrong meeting credited 0.5 correctness (should be 0). sf-05: two citations marked as not supporting a sentence they support together. pp-01 is under review: its required facts bundle the step schedule, so an answer with the asked caps scores 0.
Selection: the default-switch rule, decided before the TEST run and applied once to TEST (the rule and its numbers are recorded with the selection).

questions.question: In the minutes of the June 2018 meeting, what did participants say about the flattening yield curve?
questions.reference_answer: Participants pointed to factors other than the gradual rise of the federal funds rate that could narrow the spread between long-term and short-term Treasury yields, such as lower estimates of the longer-run neutral real rate, lower longer-term inflation expectations, or lower term premiums. A number of participants thought it important to keep monitoring the slope of the yield curve, given that an inverted yield curve has indicated an increased risk of recession; participants also discussed a staff indicator of recession likelihood based on the spread between the current federal funds rate and its expected level several quarters ahead, and several cautioned that yield curve movements should be read within the broader context of financial conditions and the outlook.
required_facts: participants pointed to factors other than the gradual rise of the federal funds rate that could reduce the spread between long-term and short-term Treasury yields
A number of participants thought it would be important to continue to monitor the slope of the yield curve, given that an inverted yield curve has indicated an increased risk of recession

Several participants cautioned that yield curve movements should be interpreted within the broader context of financial conditions and the outlook

questions.question: According to the minutes of the April 2020 meeting, what did the staff forecast for output and unemployment, and what gloomier scenario did they weigh?
questions.reference_answer: The staff's April 2020 projection was downgraded notably from March: U.S. real GDP was forecast to plummet and the unemployment rate to soar in the second quarter, and, under baseline assumptions that restrictions would ease gradually, real GDP was forecast to rise appreciably and the unemployment rate to decline considerably in the second half of the year, though a complete recovery was not expected by year-end. The staff judged that a more pessimistic projection, with a second wave of the coronavirus outbreak and renewed strict restrictions beginning around year-end, was no less plausible than the baseline forecast.

answer.text:
According to the minutes of the April 28-29, 2020 meeting, the staff forecast that U.S. real GDP would “plummet” and the unemployment rate would “soar” in the second quarter of that year, with real GDP “rise appreciably” and the unemployment rate “decline considerably” in the second half of the year, although “a complete recovery was not expected by year-end.” [1]

They also weighed a more pessimistic scenario in which a second wave of the coronavirus outbreak, with another round of strict restrictions on social interactions and business operations, would begin “around year-end,” causing real GDP to decrease, the unemployment rate to jump, and inflation to face renewed downward pressure next year. [1] Compared with the baseline, that scenario had more severe and protracted disruption, with real GDP and inflation lower and the unemployment rate higher by the end of the medium-term projection. [1]

answer.text:
Per the March 2021 staff outlook, the American Rescue Plan Act was described as “considerably larger than what the staff had assumed in the January projection,” and the staff said that, taken together with other factors, real GDP growth was projected to be “substantial this year” and the unemployment rate was forecast to decline markedly [1]. The staff also said inflation was expected to be temporarily boosted this year by “the expected emergence of some production bottlenecks and supply constraints,” with the 12-month changes in total and core PCE prices expected to transitorily move above 2 percent in coming months [1]. 

The March minutes also say the staff saw upside inflation risks as having increased since the previous forecast and now viewed the risks to the inflation projection as balanced [2].

questions.question: What did the minutes of the March 2024 meeting say about slowing down the shrinking of the Fed's balance sheet, and was anything decided?
questions.reference_answer: The minutes of the March 19-20, 2024 meeting say no decisions about adjusting the pace of balance sheet runoff were made. The vast majority of participants judged it would be prudent to begin slowing the pace of runoff fairly soon, and participants generally favored reducing the monthly pace by roughly half, keeping the agency MBS cap and adjusting the redemption cap on Treasury securities; a few participants preferred to continue the current pace until market indicators showed reserves approaching ample.

answer.text:
At the March 19-20, 2024 meeting, participants discussed slowing the pace of balance sheet runoff consistent with the Committee’s May 2022 plans, which said the Committee intends to slow and then stop the decline in the balance sheet when reserve balances are somewhat above the level judged consistent with ample reserves [1]. Participants broadly judged it would be appropriate to take a cautious approach, and the vast majority thought it would be prudent to begin slowing the pace of runoff fairly soon; they said a slower pace would help the Committee assess market conditions, give banks and funding markets more time to adjust, and reduce the probability of money markets experiencing undue stress [2].

No decision to adjust the pace of runoff was made at that meeting [1]. The passage says the discussions were intended to help inform the Committee’s future decisions about how and when to slow runoff, but it does not say the Committee decided then to slow it [1].

questions.question: Before the June 2016 vote, how did FOMC participants and staff see the UK referendum on leaving the European Union affecting markets and the outlook?
questions.reference_answer: As of July 10, 2016, the minutes of the June 14-15, 2016 meeting (released July 6) were the latest record. The staff reported that the expected federal funds rate path had flattened partly because of growing investor concerns about the British referendum on membership in the European Union, that Treasury yields moved lower late in the period amid those concerns, and that uncertainty about the outcome seemed to be holding down investment in the United Kingdom. Most participants noted that the referendum could generate financial market turbulence that could adversely affect domestic economic performance, and participants generally thought it prudent to wait for the outcome before adjusting policy.

questions.question: So far, when do Fed officials expect to start shrinking the balance sheet, and do they agree on the timing?

questions.question: Why did the FOMC decide to raise rates at its December 2016 meeting?
questions.reference_answer: As of December 20, 2016 the explanation rests on the December 14, 2016 statement, since the minutes were not yet released: in view of realized and expected labor market conditions and inflation, the Committee raised the target range for the federal funds rate to 1/2 to 3/4 percent. The November 2016 minutes had already shown most participants thought an increase could well become appropriate relatively soon.

questions.question: As of late October 2021, has the Fed started tapering its asset purchases yet, and what had it signaled about timing?
questions.reference_answer: No. As of October 31, 2021 the Committee had not begun tapering: at its September 2021 meeting it was still increasing holdings of Treasury securities by at least $80 billion per month and agency mortgage-backed securities by at least $40 billion per month, and said that if progress continued broadly as expected, a moderation in the pace of asset purchases may soon be warranted. The September minutes (released October 13) state that no decision to proceed with a moderation was made, that participants generally saw a gradual tapering concluding around the middle of next year as likely appropriate, and that if a decision came at the next meeting, tapering could commence with the monthly purchase calendars beginning in either mid-November or mid-December.

questions.question: Why did the Fed raise the interest it pays banks on reserves in June 2021 even though it wasn't hiking rates?
questions.reference_answer: With money market rates under downward pressure, the Board of Governors voted unanimously at the June 2021 meeting to raise the interest rates on required and excess reserve balances to 0.15 percent, 15 basis points above the bottom of the unchanged target range, to foster trading in the federal funds market at rates well within the target range and to support the smooth functioning of short-term funding markets. Participants agreed this technical adjustment had no bearing on the appropriate path for the federal funds rate or the stance of monetary policy.

Hard negatives: minutes-2021-07-28#0037 (IORB rate established at 0.15 percent, July) and minutes-2020-03-15#0030 (lowered to 0.10 percent). minutes-2021-07-28#0015 (EFFR rose 4 basis points after the June increase in the IOER and ON RRP rates) is also a next-meeting recap. answer.text:
The October 2015 statement said the Committee would decide at its next meeting whether it would be appropriate to raise the target range by assessing progress toward maximum employment and 2 percent inflation, using a wide range of information.[1] It also said the Committee anticipated that it would be appropriate to raise the target range when it had seen some further improvement in the labor market and was reasonably confident inflation would move back to its 2 percent objective over the medium term.[1]

questions.reference_answer: At the September 2020 meeting, where the Committee kept the target range at 0 to 1/4 percent and adopted outcome-based forward guidance, Robert S. questions.question: By how much did the FOMC decide in November 2021 to scale back its monthly bond buying, and was the vote unanimous?
questions.reference_answer: At its November 2-3, 2021 meeting the Committee decided to begin reducing the monthly pace of its net asset purchases by $10 billion for Treasury securities and $5 billion for agency mortgage-backed securities, so that beginning later that month it would increase its holdings by at least $70 billion per month of Treasury securities and at least $35 billion per month of agency mortgage-backed securities. The vote was unanimous: all 11 voting members voted for the action and none voted against.

the vote was unanimous, with 11 members voting for the action and none against

Derived tally: Powell, Williams, Barkin, Bostic, Bowman, Brainard, Clarida, Daly, Evans, Quarles, Waller = 11 for; minutes #0028 'Voting against this action: None.' Minutes #0025 is the directive ($70 billion and $35 billion from mid-November). Minutes #0020 (participants supported the $10/$5 billion plan) is supporting. questions.question: What did the FOMC approve in its October 11, 2019 notation vote to keep reserves ample, and did those steps change the stance of policy?
questions.reference_answer: By notation vote completed on October 11, 2019, the Committee approved steps to keep the supply of reserves ample: the Federal Reserve would purchase Treasury bills at least into the second quarter of next year (2020) to maintain over time ample reserve balances at or above the level that prevailed in early September 2019, and would conduct term and overnight repurchase agreement operations at least through January of next year. The Committee said these actions were purely technical measures that did not represent a change in the stance of monetary policy.
